lesson.title: Crossing Borders: How Traffic Moves Between Networks
lesson.summary: Interdomain routing is routing between autonomous systems, where BGP's policy driven path vector approach replaces the shared cost metrics and full trust that intradomain routing relies on.
lesson.body:
Interdomain routing is the routing problem on the other side of that boundary: how traffic finds its way between autonomous systems, across organizational borders where none of the cooperative assumptions that make intradomain routing simple can be relied on anymore. No autonomous system can assume another AS will honestly flood its internal topology, none can assume the other wants to minimize the same cost metric, and none can assume the relationship is purely technical rather than commercial. BGP, built on path vector routing, is the only protocol actually used for this job across the real internet, precisely because it was designed around those constraints rather than around finding a mathematically shortest path.

The practical difference in behavior between the two layers is significant. Inside an AS, OSPF or a similar interior protocol chases one answer, the lowest cost path by some agreed metric, and every router is expected to arrive at a mutually consistent view of that answer. Between autonomous systems, BGP routers exchange AS paths, and each network applies its own, potentially completely different, policy to decide what to accept, prefer, and re-advertise, so it is entirely normal and expected for two neighboring autonomous systems to disagree about which route is best, because best is defined locally, not globally. A route that one AS is happy to accept from a customer, it will typically advertise onward to all of its own neighbors, because carrying that traffic is exactly what it is paid to do, while a route learned from a peer is usually only advertised onward to that AS's own customers, not to its other peers or providers, since there is no business reason to do a competitor's or a partner's transit work for free. That kind of asymmetric, relationship dependent behavior has no equivalent inside a single AS running OSPF, and it is the direct consequence of interdomain routing needing to encode business relationships, developed further when looking at peering and transit, rather than just network topology.

Interdomain routing is also, necessarily, the layer where the internet's scale is actually managed. A BGP router does not need, and could not handle, a complete map of every router on the internet, it only needs to know, for each destination prefix, which of its neighboring autonomous systems offers a usable path and how that path compares under its own policy. That is a direct payoff of the AS abstraction: interdomain routing operates over a graph whose nodes are entire autonomous systems, a set that is large but still dramatically smaller than the set of every individual router and link inside all of them, which is the only reason path vector routing at internet scale is tractable at all.
